utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: And you will call witness...

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Irina Kacic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to thank the legal officers of the Registry for kindly helping us; I wonder whether you feel that we should now have the appearances again, or can we do it without that? Not necessary. All right. So we move on. While we are waiting for the witness, may I take this opportunity to ask the Prosecution whether the Witness C has dropped out?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Ms. Kacic. I would like to ask you to make the solemn declaration. IRINA KACIC (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is your full name Irina Kacic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Moslavena in Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And that is in the Republic of Croatia, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 21st December 1951.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did you do most of your schooling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And prior to 1991 where did you live during your adult life?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is your nationality Croatian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what is your religion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am Catholic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Prior to 1991 were you married?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When were you married? What year?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And who did you marry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Petar, Petar Kacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And as a result of that marriage did you have any children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And how many children did you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Three.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what were the sexes of the children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A son and two daughters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During the siege of Vukovar in 1991, where were you staying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First we were in the basement in our house, and after that in a shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the basement of your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until 15th September.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And why did you leave the basement of your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because our flat was hit during the heaviest raid at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And where did you move to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We moved to a public nuclear shelter in the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in the public nuclear shelter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until Vukovar fell, that is 19th November.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And on 19th November, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We left the shelter and headed towards the hospital. (12.30 pm)

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Why did you go to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because the army was in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what did you expect to happen at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were expecting that that would be the safest way to leave town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And who did you go to the hospital with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went with my children and the other people from the shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And when you say your children, do you mean your three children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What about your husband?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My husband was killed on 2nd October.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is of 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And how was he killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was killed in battle. He was a commander in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And when you went to the hospital, where did you go? What part of the hospital did you go to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had to enter the building and we climbed to the first floor, though it was all damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And was this on the day of the 19th of November 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At about what time did you get there on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Around midday. Maybe in the early afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And after you arrived there what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the army arrived at the building in the yard the order was issued that all the civilians had to leave the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And was it said where they had to go, if they left the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To Velepromet, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, did you go to Velepromet on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I stayed in the hospital with the children.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And why did you stay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because Dr. Bosanac sent a message to say that we could stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, did anything else happen on that day that you can recollect now? That is the 19th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing in particular. We had to go downstairs where the wounded were, and we were expected to stay there and wait to see what would happen next.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what happened next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we got there it was already night, and then gradually people in uniform came in and called out the names of our men, Croats, mainly soldiers. They banged on the door. It was dark. We could not see exactly who it was, but anyway, they were calling out these people by name, because they thought that they were hiding in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, these people that were in uniform, were they on the Serb side or the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you know -- you said they were in uniform. What uniforms were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly uniforms of the Yugoslav army, the grey uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were there other uniforms other than uniforms of the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They also had some of their own camouflage uniforms, some of the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And when people were called out, do you know what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not see, but I think that they did not find any of those whose names they called.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, did this occur during the evening, during the night-time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And this is the night of 19th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The night between 19th and 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, what happened on the next day, the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next day in the morning we were given orders to abandon the hospital, or rather to go out, and we headed towards the exit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, who gave you those orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly who gave the orders, but in any event, that was the message that we received in our room, and people suddenly started moving towards the exit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And when you say, "we moved towards the exit", was it you and your family, your three children, as well as the other people in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Other people as well. Myself and the children and other people of course, those who were mobile, not the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And where did you move to with your children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I headed towards the exit with the children and then we saw that something was happening there, that they were separating the men from the women, and when I got to the door I saw Mr. Sljivancanin. We stood in front of him. He just pointed that I and the daughters had to go to one side, and that my son had to go to another.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How did you know it was Major Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that moment I did not know, but I later learned his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what happened when your son was separated from you and your two daughters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just managed to address myself to Sljivancanin. I said that he was a child, and that he should not be separated, and he said that he would check everything. I just managed to give him his documents and take from him his bag and we were separated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And when you say, "give him his documents and take from him his bag", you are talking about your son, are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes. My son.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened after your son -- after this was -- after Sljivancanin said that he would check it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing happened. They did not check anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did you go? Where did you and your two daughters go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I and my two daughters went to the right where I was told to go, and then we waited to be sent somewhere. We had to wait. They said we should form groups, one group that wanted to go to Croatia, another group that wanted to stay in the hospital, and a third group that wanted to go to any third countries. We chose Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Could you see what was happening to your son at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very briefly. We just saw that they were standing against the wall and they were probably being searched to see whether they had any objects. This was very briefly. After that we did not see them because they went towards the exit to the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And was your view obstructed then, once he went to the other side, the exit on the other side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, we could not see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So you could not see him after that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Did I not see him after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what then happened to you? What was the next thing that happened to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We waited for several more hours in this small group in the hospital compound, and then buses came to fetch us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And where were you taken by the buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The buses drove us in the direction of Negoslavci, from Vukovar to Negoslavci. That direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what happened? Where did you end up ultimately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the end we arrived in Sremska Mitrovica. We spent the night there, and then the second day we went to Croatia through Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, after you left the hospital in these buses, did you see your son again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you make enquiries about where your son was after you got back to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, immediately. As soon as we got to Croatia we asked where the people who had been taken away from the hospital were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you -- were you able to find anything out about his whereabouts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was your son's name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Igor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what was his date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 23rd August 1975.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So at the time he was 16, was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How tall was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was tall, about 1 metre 90.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, on the last day that you saw him there at the hospital, can you give us a description of how he was dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. He had jeans on, a jacket which was then called a college jacket, an American wind breaker. He had a T-shirt underneath. That is all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What about his shoes? What sort of shoes did he have on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tennis shoes. White tennis shoes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did he have any other items in his possession that you knew of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had bits and pieces, like all children do. He had a little teddy. It was not a teddy, it was something like a mouse, actually, a brown mouse, and that is what we found on him, and he had another small dolphin that he had made by himself in wood and he always held it in his pocket, thinking it would bring him luck.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, I would like you to look at the photograph that I am now going to show you, and might this be placed on the ELMO, please? There is one copy for the Defence. Now, just looking at the photograph that is now on the screen beside you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you recognise that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do. That is my son.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I tender that, your Honours, and might it be given the next exhibit number in order?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 69.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Ms. Kacic, would you now please look for me at the next photograph that I show you, and it is copied for the Defence. Perhaps that could be placed on the overhead screen too, please. Ms. Kacic, I am wondering if you would look at the photograph on the machine there, actually look at the machine itself, and if you could pick up that little pointer that is there on the witness table, do you see that brown pointer? That is right. Now, on the machine, if you could look at that photograph and if you point to the things that you recognise, can you tell us what you recognise, please, in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is his key ring that we bought in Senj. This is another key ring. This is a nail cutter. These are little leather strings on which he wore a bullet, and this is his silver chain, and I do not know about the other objects. (Indicated).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And do you recognise these as items that belonged to your son?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And when did you first see these items as depicted on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we went for identification purposes in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And were you able to then make that identification in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes we, were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that photograph, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Ms. Kacic, I am now going to ask you to just look at a very short piece of video, and I might ask the technicians to hold the video in place when it is played. I will just ask you if you are able, to identify anything -- any of the things that are depicted on this video. You do not need to point to them, Ms. Kacic, because they will be on your television screen, and if you could just tell us when you see it so if that could now just be played and once we get to the scene that you identify we will then hold the screen for a moment. Can we do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. (Video played) This is the soft little mouse that he had, and this is the dolphin that he made in wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Okay. Perhaps we could just go back to the little mouse to start with just to start over again, just the mouse, and would you just hold on the mouse? Thank you. Was that a little soft toy that belonged to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. Thank you. I have no further questions, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, except for my condolences before this -- for the tragic loss of this witness, I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I assume there is no objection to the witness being released.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Ms. Kacic, the court is most grateful to you for coming to The Hague to give evidence in court. You may now be released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May I propose that we will now stand in recess until 2.30?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases. (1.00 pm) (Luncheon adjournment) 24 25 (2.30 pm)

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just thought that I would indicate at the moment what our position is regarding witnesses. We have two witnesses available for this afternoon and tomorrow we anticipate calling three witnesses, and then on Friday there is one witness, sorry, on Wednesday, so today -- two more today, three on Tuesday, and one on Wednesday and I can give your Honours the names of those but I think you probably have the list already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, so today we would hear witness number two and three.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. It is two and three on the list, and four... no, that is wrong. I have not -- I can give you the names, your Honour, which is a better -- it is the present witness in the court, Ljubas, than Radocaj, than Schou, Witness A, and then Brletic, and then Kypr. And that concludes the evidence for this week, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This witness will be taken by Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. First of all I would ask the witness to stand up and to make the solemn declaration. ANICA LJUBAS (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. First of all I understand there is a problem with the -- yes. Usual technical problem. There is some noise. I gather that we would need a few minutes, probably fifteen-twenty minutes to remedy this, to cure this problem and I wonder whether the interpreters may go on? I mean, is it really disturbing? Is it really impossible for you to work with the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It is very disturbing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So therefore we will have to take a recess of ten minutes and -- it has stopped. Oh, wonderful. So, all right. Wonderful, so you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Ms. Ljubas, could you please state to the court your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Anica Ljubas.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what is the place and date of your birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 2nd October 1948, Tomislavgrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And Tomislavgrad -- and that is in which republic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Could you tell us your nationality and your ethnic background, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you have a family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do. Three daughters and five grandchildren, and I had a son.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you give us the name of your son and when he was born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My son's name was Hrvoje Ljubas. He was born on 26th January 1971.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now I am a housewife.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Where did you live in summer 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the village of Sotin, near Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How close to Vukovar is Sotin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 10 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What was the ethnic composition of the village of Sotin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The majority population was Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, turning to the events in summer and fall 1991, on August 24th 1991, did you hear on the radio that Vukovar was attacked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what was the effect of this news? Did young men from Sotin go to Vukovar to join the defence of the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was your son going as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What was the reason that your son did not join?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because his friend had gone, and he stayed on in the village to help these people in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us the name of his friend who went instead of him to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Drazen Luketic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What happened to this person in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was killed on 24th when Dom Technike in Borovo was attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was there a funeral held in commemoration of Drazen Luketic in Sotin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On 26th. On 26th August 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you remember when this funeral took place, when in the day of this 26th August 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember very well. The funeral was supposed to be at 4 pm, and at five minutes after five aircraft bombed the funeral and the entire village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you personally see any impacts of those attacks by the planes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw parts of concrete strewn about, broken glass. On the left-hand side there was a store. It was destroyed then. Trees were uprooted, two women were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What was your impression? Were these planes in any way associated with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those were JNA aeroplanes. Those of the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: For how long did this attack, this air bombing last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was one sortie and then they bombed us and then they came back again and after that I did not see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you have an idea why the JNA attacked your village? Was there any provocation from the side of the people of Sotin, towards the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was there any warning given by the JNA to the people in Sotin before they attacked the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was there any defence in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What happened then, after the bombing you just described? Where did you sleep that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were staying at our neighbour's basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How was the night? Was it quiet or were there further attacks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Afterwards it was quiet. There were not any further attacks that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What happened the next day, August 27th? Did you again see presence of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next day we only went through the village to see what had happened, where we were, whether someone was killed, but the entire day this following day was a quiet one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you see that day, this one or the following, any tanks who had circumvented your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next day we saw tanks. I personally saw them -- 60, 80 tanks, I counted once.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, what happened in the course of the following night? Was there a time when you decided to leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next night we were informed by our neighbours and those who were guarding us, women, children, and the entire village, that they could not take care of us any longer, that we had to get ready and get out of the village because it was getting dangerous. The army was already there, so we could not stay on any longer, we had to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did most of the people in Sotin decide to leave that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The entire village was evacuated that night at 3 o'clock. The night between 28th and 29th.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You said that the majority of the people in the village of Sotin were of Croatian nationality, so there were also Serbs living in that village. Can you tell us what the reaction of those Serb people was? Did they join you in leaving the village that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I could see it was night-time. Some had left, others had not. We did not know that, because in the neighbouring village we saw that there were Serbs also who got out together with us that night, who were in the same group.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us exactly why you left the village, your home village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We left it because we were afraid. We saw what was happening, that the army was there. They were bombing us, and we were frightened and we did not dare stay any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: When was it the last time you saw your son?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 28th August 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit more? Where did you see him? In a car? What was your position at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was also in a car, in a column. We joined up with them at Ilaca on the highway towards Zagreb and I found him there and I asked him to come with me to Zagreb and he said, "mummy, no. I am going to Vukovar". And that is when we parted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I would like to show you now a picture. There are samples, also, for the Defence and your Honours. Ms. Ljubas, can you tell us, what is that person on the picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My son. He was only 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Have you seen him ever again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I would like to tender that as the next Prosecution exhibit. That is probably number 71, if I am correct.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, that is 71.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Ljubas, can you tell us where your convoy went to after you had left Sotin that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It headed towards Zagreb and some people came back because they thought that these times would pass by and that we could stay on in the village. We still had no idea what would happen to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you arrive at the village of Opatovac at a certain time in the next days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you again see JNA soldiers forces arriving at that place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what was the reaction from your side? Did you leave again this village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And where did you go to afterwards, after Opatovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went towards Sotin, along the Danube because we did not dare show up anywhere. We went through the forest all night until we reached Sotin because we knew that the army was in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you go back to your home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Where did you stay? Outside Sotin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the forest down there at Orerada.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: For how long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Three days and three nights.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was there a time afterwards that you crossed the Danube and went on to the other side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. A man took us to the other side of the Danube on a boat.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was there somebody who told you to surrender to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The man who took us by boat. He said that we should surrender and that we should not go to the forest on our own because the forest was full of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you surrender in fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you tell us briefly how that went along?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they brought us in front of a building there was some concrete and there was also something green. There were a lot of people in uniform and some in civilian clothes and we did not know who was who, but we had suspected who that was, and they were teasing us a lot, and who brought us should take us back, and I started crying and I said that I had four children and I said that if they wanted to they could kill me right there and then and I said, "I hope you will be fair and let my children go", but there was a lot of quarrelling going on, they were getting us off into a big vehicle where the army came, two soldiers came, and they put us into this big vehicle and they took us to Bac for questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: After being questioned, were you returned to Backa Palanka at a certain point. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After questioning they put us up in a village, some village out there and we stayed there until 21st or 22nd, I am not too sure what date it was, and then the next day, the day after that, we were wondering how long we would stay there on our own. No one was coming to see us after that, so we thought that we would go back to Bac to ask what would happen to us and that is exactly what happened. We went to Bac one morning and we asked how long we would be staying there and a man showed up who recognised my husband. Actually, my husband recognised him, and said, "what are you doing there?", and he said, "I do not know what we are doing here. We are here", and he invited us to his office. He offered us coffee and all that, and we asked, "what is going to happen to us now? What about us?", and he said, "as far as I am concerned you are free", and we said, "we do not dare go out because if we do not have any kind of certificate somebody will catch us again", and he said, "you can go", and he said, "where do you want to go?". We said, "we will go to Belgrade". We did not dare mention that we wanted to go to Zagreb. So we went to Bac, Backa Palanka, Pajo, Novi Sad, Sremska Mitrovica, Sid, Bijeljina, Doboj, so we reached Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you reach Zagreb at a certain point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We reached Zagreb on 16th November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I assume there is no objection to the witness being released. No objection. Ms. Ljubas, I would like to express to you the gratitude of this court for coming to The Hague to give evidence in court. Thank you so much. You may be released. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I call Duka Radocaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, I think you said before that this afternoon you would call only Ms. Ljubas and Ms. Radocaj?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Duka Radocaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Only two witnesses. We were wondering whether you could also call a third witness, because we have plenty of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I do not think he is ready, your Honour. Mr. Williamson is going to take -- Mr. Williamson is going to take that witness but I do not think we will be ready, your Honours. Whatever happens, we are going to be short today and short tomorrow and short on Wednesday, your Honour. It has been moving much faster than we anticipated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Williamson?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, just very briefly, Witness A, who would be the next witness to come, is ill today. He is suffering from the 'flu which unfortunately I think he caught from me, but anyway he is not here today. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, and so you cannot call the witness -- who on my list is number 6, on the the confidential list which was distributed to us on -- I think on Friday, last Friday. I do not know whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour, that witness is not ready to be called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I see. Thank you. I would like to ask the witness to make the solemn declaration. DUKA RADOCAJ (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is your full name Duka Radocaj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Duka Radocaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And Mr. Radocaj, what is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 12th October 1952.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Radocaj, on 4th February 1996 did Mr. Kevin Curtis from the International Criminal Tribunal visit you and obtain from you a statement of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And was that statement taken down in the English language but translated to you in the Croatian language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And after it was translated to you were you asked to sign at the bottom of each page of that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I now ask you to look at the document that is shown to you, and might it be given the next exhibit number in order, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 72.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Radocaj, can you see your signature at the bottom of each page of that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. I tender that, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Radocaj, where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And up until 1991, where did you live for the most part of your life?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my place of birth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And that is in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Lovas, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, during the hostilities in 1991 was Lovas affected by the war at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Around the end of August and early September of that year, where were you -- were you still living in Lovas at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you observe that tensions were rising considerably in and around Lovas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what did you observe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there was a lot of military people, vehicles, in the surroundings, movement was not allowed for certain periods of time, one was not allowed to go to, or travel to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And you mentioned military vehicles. Military vehicles of what army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the army that the vehicles belonged to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And you also mentioned the town of Sotin. What was the position in that town, which is near Lovas, I understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The inhabitants of Sotin, somewhere in August were evacuated. It may have been the beginning of September, but they were evacuated and some of them came to Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, around about 22nd and 23rd of September 1991, were there further refugees passing through that came to the village of Lovas from another town in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On 22nd, quite a number of people, a large number of people from Tovarnik came to Lovas, but there were people from other places as well, but especially from Tovarnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what had happened in Tovarnik to require, to have those people come to Lovas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that day the JNA attacked Tovarnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, just to assist their Honours in locating these towns, might the witness be shown Exhibit P4, which I understand is a yellow map like that. (Handed). (3.00 pm) Thank you. Could that map be placed on the overhead projector? Mr. Radocaj, I would like you to look at the map that is in front of you on the projector there and to pick up the small wooden pointer on the desk in front of you and I wonder if you would help us by pointing to some of the towns that you mention in your evidence. Firstly, can you tell us -- point to us the village of Lovas? Can you find that there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here it is. (Indicated).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. And perhaps just so everyone can be directly orientated, can you just point to the city of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vukovar is here. (Indicated).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And Ilok?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ilok is here. (Indicated).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Okay. And one of the towns that you mentioned, Sotin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here it is. Sotin. (Indicated).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And that is -- perhaps we could close in a bit on the -- can we project in a bit on that? Thank you. And another village that I believe you will mention, Mohovo. Mohovo. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is here. (Indicated).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And Tovarnik, that you were just referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Tovarnik. (Indicated).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think that will do for the moment. Thank you very much. Now, was there a very large increase in the population of Lovas after the attack by the JNA on Tovarnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that point in time, actually, on that day or the following few days, in my view the population doubled in relation to the normal situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, on the 10th October 1991, did you hear certain news which was likely to affect Lovas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly on the 10th of October. You are interested in that day only. On that day we heard news that some kind of an attack was under preparation against Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And how did you come to hear this news?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We heard of it because a local person from Tovarnik who was arrested allegedly fled from the military unit that was pursuing him, and then he brought this news from Tovarnik, or rather he alerted us across the radio, by means of the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what did you do when you heard this news of the imminent attack on Lovas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that moment, since there were no defences or anything, people gathered and discussed the issue, and shortly after that the shelling started.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: From what direction was the shelling coming into Lovas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The shelling was coming from the direction of Tovarnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, what did you do when this happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was there in the local community offices, and since there was no one I headed back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what did you do when you went home? What did you discover?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I got home there were my wife's parents and her brother, his wife, and two children staying with me, so I talked to them and I wanted to go and see my mother, who was living a little way from my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And so did you then proceed to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I started off and part of the way, maybe some 100 metres or even less, from the opposite direction, or rather from the direction that I was heading for, the firing started, that is in the direction of Opatovac. Therefore -- my street is called Mlinska, and the shooting started from the mlin, or the mill, and that mill is on the road to Opatovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you then return to your home as a result of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that I had to go back home because I felt it was not safe to proceed, so I went back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you then subsequently decide that you would try and escape from Lovas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My wife's late father said to me and my brother-in-law that we should flee.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And to where were you going to flee?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were going to the village of Mohovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived at Mohovo, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I arrived in Mohovo from the direction of my village there was daily shooting, which means from the actual village of Lovas. Then I looked for my brother-in-law, because we had got lost through the fields of corn on the way to Mohovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, once you had been in Mohovo, did you decide that it would be better for you to return to your house in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed briefly in Mohovo, and I went to Ilok at one point to look for my brother-in-law who was in Ilok, because I heard that he was there, and I went to look for him because I had decided to go back to see how the people who were in my house were faring.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you then do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And how did you get back to your house in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went back through the fields again in which mostly maize had been planted so I thought that would be the best way to get back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when you got back there, what did you discover?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, when I got back I did not find my wife and the other people at home, but my neighbour told me that my father-in-law had been killed but apparently my wife was in the village. However, that same day unfortunately she had been taken to Sid because they were mistreated in Lovas, and they tried to save themselves by staying with relatives in Dobanovci where my father-in-law had a sister.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And Dobanovci is in Serbia, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct, near Zemun.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, what was the next thing that happened? What did you do then when you discovered your wife had gone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the 13th, that was the date. On that day I spent the night outside, near the house, hiding in the maize fields which was also next to the house, and during the night I felt very cold, so I climbed into my own attic because at the time I did not know that my wife had left that same day, so I spent the night there, and in the morning, the next morning on 14th, in the direction of this village that I had mentioned, Opatovac, a convoy of military vehicles went by, tanks, trucks, jeeps, and all those other things whose names I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were these military vehicles of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To judge by the markings and the colour, rather, yes, the JNA because they were just one street away and I was watching from the attic and I saw that they were olive green/grey in colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, did you subsequently decide to go to the co-operative building in Lovas and to, in effect, turn yourself in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. A soldier picked me up because in the meantime my mother had reached my house and a soldier saw me there talking to my mother, and he picked us up and took me to a house in the neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He took me to a local person and asked this local man whether he knew me, and then they took me to the local co-operative where I had to register and I was ordered to come tomorrow at 7 o'clock, to come to work in that co-operative, the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you do that the next day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was forced to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what sort of work did you perform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All kinds of jobs, from feeding livestock, harvesting the corn, and similar jobs, depending on what the person in charge told me to do. Of course, these jobs and all other local people were done by us under the watchful eye of the soldiers, or armed people or some local people under arms. There were some local people as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you continue this until the 17th October?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly. Until 17th October. That is what I did until then, and on that day orders were issued to the effect that no one was allowed to go home, that there would be some kind of a meeting within the compound of the co-operative.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And was there a meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The meeting unfortunately was not held. It was not held because the gentleman who were supposed to hold the meeting, his name is Ljuban Devetak, he did not show up that day for the meeting. However, a day or two later I heard that he was in Ilok, that is what his driver told me, that he was escorting the convoy because on 17th October a convoy of citizens of Ilok had left, heading towards Croatia, Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when you went to this meeting where Mr. Devetak did not turn up or did not arrive, were you addressed by a person in military uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were several persons. One was called "Captain", and there were several soldiers. They put weapons in front of us and I saw a submachinegun among these weapons and there were also automatic rifles there, the ones they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did this person called "Captain" tell you why you had been locked up? Did this person called "Captain" say to you why you had been locked up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That captain said to us that allegedly some of the locals were shooting at his soldiers, and if there would be no shooting that night, at us, that then he would know that it was us who did the shooting, and that we would be in trouble then and then he added, "even if that does not happen you are going to be in trouble, definitely".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And so what happened? What did they do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That night on 17th, we had to sit on wooden benches all night with our hands on our backs like this. (Indicated). Very often people were not even allowed to move, because one of these people were walking around, and if anyone would move they would hit him with their hands and with other objects.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, what did they do to you the next morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not even underline that. That night they did not even allow people to go to the toilet or anything, and in the morning at one point, it seemed -- well, they had given us a few packs of cigarettes, so we lit a cigarette or two, those people who were smokers, and after that Devetak came with a group of bodyguards or soldiers or paramilitary soldiers, whatever they may be, and they started beating up all the people. Actually, before that, they had separated a group that was supposed to be some kind of work group. They were in charge of the electricity, but there was not any electricity, and also the waterworks were down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when you say they started beating you, what did they beat you with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With everything that was available. That is to say, starting from rifles, that is to say rifle butts, various bars, then batons, their hands, some kind of wooden sticks, et cetera, and they would even put their knives into people's thighs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, a little later did they bring in a group of four or five people who -- villagers -- who they said had failed to attend a meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what did they do to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They put those people in front of a wall, in front of us -- but I should have said before this, that a group of some 20 people were put aside compared to the place where we had spent the night and they brought these people in front of this wall of this workshop that was within this co-operative, and they were beating them in particular because allegedly they did not respond to the invitation to come to this meeting, so these people were especially mistreated. I do not know how to put this. These people were really tortured. They stuck knives into them, they beat them up, this wall was all bloody.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: A little later on were you then picked out and told that you would be taken to a vineyard to pick grapes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That came afterwards. They said that we would go to pick grapes, and they lined us up as we were supposed to leave the village, we were supposed to go to the farm that was at the outskirts of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did they say anything to you about land mines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No one had told us a thing about land mines. Only on the way they said that if it was mined, that we had laid those mines and that we would lose our lives. They said something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unfortunately we were forced into this minefield, and in my opinion we only had dear God to thank for the fact that a military vehicle came by and in it was some kind of officer, JNA officer. It was a jeep or something of the sort, some kind of military vehicle, but unfortunately too late, because several people were already killed in this minefield, and they were shot in the back from automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did anyone actually fall upon mines when you were in the field?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were spread out as far as my arms can stretch. I mean, that far. And a boy was killed by a mine, allegedly, but later people who were standing closer to this boy told me that one of the soldiers had pushed him onto that mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did they tell you to do anything with your feet when you were in the minefield?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They said that we should move our legs like when you are cutting the grass or clover, that we should make it that kind of movement with our feet as we were moving along.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you say this JNA jeep arrived with an officer. What happened? What did they do when they arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know to what extent you can imagine all of this, because we were all confused, frightened. They were quarreling between themselves and this officer ordered these people to be taken out. I mean, these people who were still alive or those who were wounded, to get them out of the field. Actually, I was the first one, and other people also de-mined the field, according to the orders issued by a soldier who was acting upon orders of that officer who was in the vehicle. We had to de-mine -- we had to take these mines away by hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And how were you told to do that? Did they tell you how to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This officer ordered this soldier and since I was the first one there who had to de-mine, the soldier gave me instructions how I was supposed to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what did he tell you to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since I am no soldier, no expert in this field, I mean, I had only served in the previous army, he told me that, to come to some kind of stick that was there in the minefield in that field, and to pull it towards myself, and to get this little wire off this stick, and then we went to another one and then we cut this wire because in the meantime somebody had given me that nail cutter which I used to cut that wire.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, where were the soldiers standing when you were cutting through the wire of the mine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The soldier was standing up on the road, above this field.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, the soldiers that had taken you out from Lovas to the minefield, were they regular JNA? Did you recognise them as regular JNA soldiers, or were they some other force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not. I did not know any of these people, and now whether it was regular army or... how do you put this... whether they were reservists, I do not know, but they all had uniforms on. Those who were forcing us into the field, we are talking about that, right? (3.30 pm)

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did they have any insignia on them to indicate that they were JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had those five-pointed stars, red five-pointed stars embroidered, some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the people that arrived in the jeep, were they dressed similarly, in a similar way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The soldier was wearing an olive green/grey uniform whereas the previous ones had that light green camouflage uniform on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, once you had finished de-mining and you had de-mined a mine yourself, what happened then? What was the next thing that happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then one of the soldiers who had stayed on with us ordered me to go and have a look at the people who remained lying dead in the field, to go and check whether any one of them was still alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did, and I went from one to another, and I did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that the few of us who were left were taken back to the yard where we had set out for this minefield in the first place. These soldiers escorted us to that yard, and when we came, the other ones who had massacred those people before we went out to the minefields reappeared and I remember one of them even by name, his name was Petronije and he had an axe, and he wanted to kill all the rest of us who had remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But that did not happen. You were taken -- you ultimately went back to the co-operative building. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because then there was a man who gave them orders that they were not allowed to do anything to us, because, on the other side was a kitchen and a dining room for these people who were employed at the co-operative and they were quarreling out there and this man hid us there in the workshop and he did not allow these men to come up to us any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, I think after that you continued to do forced labour from the co-operative building until 22nd December 1991. What happened on 22nd December 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that 22nd of December in the morning we were going to work, how should I put this, there was a policeman there, a military policeman, and one of these volunteers of Devetak was there and they took us to the local police there, that they had set up. That is where I was searched as soon as I arrived. Of course, I forgot to say this, they had tied my hands in the back. When they arrested me they brought me there, they searched my pockets, and one of these people there who was some kind of commander of this police, he started beating me up, and he kicked me with his boot up here in the face, and then he kicked me between the legs and in various other ways, and this military policeman was there too who had brought me there with those two other guys. After that I was taken to the basement where they beat me all day. They tied my hands up this way, they were stretched out, they beat me in different ways, they put salt in my mouth, they beat me with different objects, with their batons, with their hands, they kicked me with their feet, they cut my teeth. At one point, as it was getting dark, that is to say I was there from the morning until late in the afternoon, it was already getting dark, they wanted to use a drilling machine in order to drill a hole through my leg but they did not have the right kind of power to do that, because something was wrong with their power generator, so they did not drill through my foot. They only drilled through my shoe, and the drilling machine had only touched my flesh very little, and of course they continued to beat me up until sometime during the night, and then this Milosevic, I think, that was the name of this commander, Milosevic, he gave orders to have my mother brought in, and that my mother would have to watch me being cut up, and when they went to pick her up these policemen said that she would have to -- that -- or rather that they told her that I would have to watch her, you know, I mean the other way around, that I would be watching my mother being cut up and they told my mother that she would be watching me being cut up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did they do anything to your teeth with pliers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I said a moment ago, they tried to cut my teeth. They cut about five teeth with pliers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How did they do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those are pliers used to cut the teeth of pigs. These are small pliers which have special cutters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know where I should begin now. From this cutting of my teeth or this situation with my mother?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, sorry, did they bring your mother to the police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did. They brought my mother and they tied her up, also with handcuffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, what did they do then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After a while -- there was no electricity, as I said. Something had gone wrong with the generator. I heard some crying or moans, I do not know how to put it, because they were bringing another man to this same cellar where I was throughout that day, and this man was Manojlo Filic. After that they brought in two other men, Mato Madarevic, and Vjekoslav Balic. They continued to beat us all that night until the morning. There were four men there and my mother, so they beat us until the morning. It had already dawned. They took away my watch so I did not know what time it was, but it was daylight already, one could see a little through the windows of the cellar. Then they let my mother go, and they continued to beat us that day, and that was already 23rd December.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, did you then -- did your cousin's husband, a Serb, come to the police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the night my cousin's husband was apprehended because he did not agree with them torturing me, because he had heard I was being tortured, and so he disagreed and then they locked him up too, and then one of his friends who were in the army went to find his brother in Tovarnik as we knew each other through football connections, and so he came to see me and said that he would save me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And were you subsequently saved as a result of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not straight away, but on 26th, because after these events of 22nd and 23rd, we were released in the night of the 23rd. I stayed home. I could not move. I could not eat, I could not do anything, so this man came on 26th, and he drove me to Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And from Bijeljina, did you then manage to get to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From Bijeljina I managed to reach Sarajevo. The road that was covered by my wife as well, as I had heard, this man who saved me gave me a telephone number, the number of the people where my wife was staying, and these people, since I arrived at night in Sarajevo, in the morning they immediately took me to see a doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And then ultimately did you manage to get to Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next day I arrived in Zagreb, and I was treated at the clinical centre in Rebro, Zagreb, and as a consequence of this beating my eardrum had been pierced from the blows, so I was also operated on in March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I assume there is no objection to the witness being released. Thank you. Thank you so much for coming here to testify. You may be released. Thank you. (The witness withdrew) So I understand that -- tomorrow we will hear three witnesses, and one on Wednesday. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. The witness on Wednesday has to be heard on Wednesday because we have to book Czech interpreters. That has been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, but may I just take a few minutes of your time? I wonder whether you intend to call other witnesses in March, because we have here a list which was distributed on the 29th January, and there are about -- more than six witnesses listed for March.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I understand all of them relate to exhumations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The exhumation part of the case your Honour, yes. There may be one witness on international armed conflict, but other than that, they all relate to the exhumation, and the investigator, which will be the concluding witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. That means that probably in March you may also be able to make your closing statement, in that week of March. We have five working days in March.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, we will not make our closing statement until the end of the case, your Honour, not until the end of the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. You are right. Sorry, I was wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But we can close our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Close your case, that is what I meant. Thank you for correcting me. So you may close your case in, therefore, in that week of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. That is our intention, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So therefore we can start with -- I wonder whether Mr. Fila will be ready to start in April. In April I think we have eight working days.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I will be ready, your Honour. I would like to say that I would finish in April, but just in case something might happen, so I would like to have some days in reserve, but judging by the number of witnesses I should be able to complete my case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. If there are no other questions, we may now stand in recess until tomorrow morning at 9.15. (4.50 pm)
